analysis.one_liner: Bans new sale, manufacture, and import of semiautomatic assault weapons and magazines holding over 15 rounds.
analysis.headline: 194 House Democrats cosponsored the bill, but the Republican-run Judiciary Committee never scheduled a markup or vote, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal crime to import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity ammunition magazines as defined in the bill, with exemptions for law enforcement, retired officers, nuclear-material security, and a long list of hunting and sporting firearms named in an appendix. People who already legally owned a covered weapon or magazine could keep it, and could sell or transfer a grandfathered weapon only through a licensed dealer after a background check. Covered guns would need secure storage around prohibited persons and date-of-manufacture markings, and local governments could use existing federal grant money to run buy-back programs.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people in communities exposed to mass shootings, since the bill cuts off the future supply of the semiautomatic rifles, pistols, and shotguns it defines and of magazines holding more than 15 rounds. Current legal owners are largely protected: they keep their weapons and can still sell or transfer a grandfathered weapon through a dealer. Police and retired officers are exempt.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People exposed to mass shootings with these weapons

how_it_helps.text: Makes it a federal crime to import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess semiautomatic assault weapons and magazines holding more than 15 rounds, stopping future additions to the domestic supply [S2][S3].

Grandfathers weapons and magazines people already lawfully own, and allows continued sale or transfer of a grandfathered weapon through a licensed dealer with a background check, so the burden on existing owners is limited [S2][S3].

Requires secure storage of grandfathered weapons where a prohibited person could reach them, serial numbers on new magazines, date-of-manufacture markings, and lets state and local governments use Byrne grant funds to pay people who surrender covered weapons in buy-backs [S2][S3].
Exemts a long list of hunting and sporting rifles and shotguns by name, plus bolt, pump, lever, and slide-action guns, antiques, and rimfire-only firearms [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Firearms manufacturers lose the ability to make and sell the covered rifles, pistols, shotguns, and magazines. Licensed dealers lose those new-sale revenues. Buyers of the covered weapons can no longer purchase them new, and owners of grandfathered large-capacity magazines can keep them but can never sell or transfer them.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun makers, dealers, and buyers of covered weapons

drawbacks.text: The definitions are broad: a semiautomatic rifle counts as an assault weapon if it has a detachable magazine plus any single feature such as a pistol grip, threaded barrel, or barrel shroud, which sweeps in many common firearms, and covered pistols and shotguns are similarly defined by feature combinations [S3].

The grandfather clause means the millions of covered weapons and magazines already in private hands stay legal and, for weapons, remain transferable through dealers, so the bill's effect on street availability depends on slow attrition rather than removal [S2][S3].

Possession itself becomes a crime for weapons not grandfathered, and violations carry forfeiture of the weapon or device, which opponents view as criminalizing ownership rather than only commerce [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's main benefit is cutting off future supply of the weapons most often used in high-casinality mass shootings, and it tries to limit the cost to current owners through grandfathering, dealer-mediated transfers, and named exemptions for hunting and sporting guns. The honest trade-off is that the existing stock is untouched and the feature-based definitions are sweeping, so the near-term public-safety gain is modest while the burden on manufacturers and some owners is real. Whether the ban meaningfully reduces gun deaths is genuinely debated; the 1994 federal ban's effects were contested, and a similar result would be possible here.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Judiciary Committee for the entire two-year Congress — no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. David Cicilline introduced the bill on February 1, 2023, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee [S1][S5].
194 House Democrats cosponsored it, the overwhelming majority of the Democratic caucus [S4].
In June 2023, Rep. Lucy McBath took over as first sponsor so she could continue adding cosponsors [S5].
The House action history shows no further activity after that: the committee never reported the bill and the full House never voted on it before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearms manufacturers and dealers are better off: they kept selling the covered semiautomatic rifles, pistols, and large-capacity magazines without any federal restriction, and current owners kept their weapons unchanged. The bill's supporters gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: All 194 cosponsors were Democrats — 90% of the 216-member caucus — and no Republican signed on; with Republicans chairing the Judiciary Committee, the bill never advanced.

industries.industry: Firearms manufacturers (semiautomatic rifles, pistols, and magazines)
industries.note: The bill outlaws new manufacture and sale of the covered weapons and of magazines holding more than 15 rounds, cutting off a large and growing part of the market; it grandfathered existing stock, so the industry keeps the value of guns already sold. Its interest in continuing unrestricted sales runs against the bill's aim of reducing the supply of these weapons.

Dealers lose new-sale revenue on covered weapons, but the bill requires grandfathered assault weapons to change hands only through a licensed dealer with a background check, steering a stream of transfer business to them.
The bill explicitly lists hundreds of hunting, target, and competition rifles and shotguns as exempt, so sales of those models continue and could even pick up demand shifted away from banned models.
